# Summary and questions
This post is to review the effective Hamiltonian framework and try to explain why certain Hamiltonians models are important in matterial physics.


# Effective Hamiltonian

Given a free Hamiltonian $H_0$ and an interacting Hamiltonian $H = H_0 + \varepsilon V$, where $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}$.

:::{#def-gap .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition of spectral gap
Consider the eigenspectrum of $H_0$ within a connected interval $\mathcal{I}_0 = [a,b] \subset \mathbb{R}$. Let the corresponding eigensubspace be denoted by $\mathcal{P}_0$, and its projection operator by $P_0$.
We say that there is a spectral gap $\Delta \in \mathbb{R}$ above $\mathcal{I}_0$ if and only if for all $\lambda, \mu \in \text{spec}(H_0)$ such that $\lambda \in \mathcal{I}_0$ and $\mu \notin \mathcal{I}_0$, we have $|\lambda - \mu| \geq \Delta$.
:::

If the interaction of $V$ on $H_0$ is small enough, this section of eigenspectrum of $H_0$ will be close to that of $H$. 
To be rigorous, consider the eigenspectrum of $H$ within the connected interval $\mathcal{I} := [a-\Delta/2, b+\Delta/2]$. 
Let eigensubspace of $H$ that supports on $\mathcal{I}$ be denoted by $\mathcal{P}$, and its projection operator by $P$.
Denote the operator norm $\|A\| := \sup_{\|\psi\|=1} \|A\ket{\psi}\|$ (maximum singular value of $A$).
For small enough $\varepsilon$, the subspace $\mathcal{P}$ will contain all those perturbed eigenvectors that are derived from $\mathcal{P}_0$. 
This is validated by @lem-subspace-proximity and @lem-direct-rotation, whose proof can be found in @bravyi2011schrieffer.

:::{#lem-subspace-proximity .callout-important icon="false"}
## Proximity of perturbed and unperturbed subspaces (@bravyi2011schrieffer, Lemma 3.1)
$|\varepsilon|\cdot \|V\| < \Delta/2 \Rightarrow \|P_0 - P\| <1$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch (Click to expand)

Define $T = P - P_0$ and $Q_0 = \mathbb{I} - P_0$, $Q = \mathbb{I} - P$. Since $T$ is Hermitian and $T^2$ is block-diagonal with respect to $P_0, Q_0$, one has
$$
\begin{align}
P_0 T^2 P_0 &= P_0 (P + P_0 - 2 P P_0) P_0 = P_0 - P_0 P P_0 = P_0 Q P_0,\\
Q_0 T^2 Q_0 &= Q_0 (P + P_0 - 2 P P_0) Q_0 = Q_0 P Q_0,
\end{align}
$$
so that $\|T\| = \sqrt{\|T^2\|} = \max(\|P_0 Q\|, \|Q_0 P\|)$, here we use the fact that $\|T^2\| = \|T\|^2$ and all vector with eigenvalue $0$ for $P_0$($Q_0$) shall be eigenvector with eigenvalue $0$ for $P_0QP_0$($Q_0PQ_0$).

Without loss of generality assume $\|T\| = \|P_0 Q\|$. Define $A = P_0 H_0 P_0$, $B = QHQ$, $X = P_0 Q$, and $Y = -\varepsilon P_0 V Q$. Use the fact that $[Q,H] = 0$ and $[P_0, H_0] = 0$, then $X$ satisfies the **Sylvester equation**:
$$
\begin{align*}
AX \!-\! XB = (P_0 H_0 P_0) (P_0 Q) \!-\! (P_0 Q) (Q H Q) = P_0 H_0 Q \!-\! P_0 H Q = \!-\varepsilon P_0 V Q := Y,
\end{align*}
$$
![](specplot.svg){#fig-specplot width=70%}
The spectra of $A$ and $B$ (viewed as operators on their respective subspaces) are separated by a gap of width $\Delta/2$ when $|\varepsilon| < \Delta/2\|V\|$. By a standard result on Sylvester equations, this spectral separation yields:
$$
\|T\| = \|X\| \leq \frac{2}{\Delta}\|Y\| \leq \frac{2}{\Delta}\|\varepsilon V\| < 1. \qquad \square
$$
:::

In the proof, we use the famous result on Sylvester equation.

:::{#thm-sylvester .callout-important icon="false"}
## (Sylvester equation)
Given two matrices $A, B$ and a matrix $X$, the Sylvester equation $AX - XB = Y$ has unique solution $X$ if and only if the eigenvalues of $A$ and $B$ are disjoint. Furthermore,
$X$ can be caluclated through: 
$$
X = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_\Gamma (zI-A)^{-1} Y (zI-B)^{-1} \,dz = -\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}A^nYB^{-n-1},
$$
where $\Gamma$ is a closed contour in the complex plane that encloses the eigenvalues of $A$ and $B$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof (Click to expand)
use evctorizaiton $\mathrm{vec}(A) = A_{ji} \ket{i}\bra{j}$ and identity $\mathrm{vec}(AXB) = (B^T \otimes A)\mathrm{vec}(X)$, then the Sylvester equation can be written as:
$$
\begin{align*}
(\mathbb{I}_n \otimes A - B^T \otimes \mathbb{I}_m)\mathrm{vec}(X) = \mathrm{vec}(Y),
\end{align*}
$$
Thsi linear equation has unique solution $\mathrm{vec}(X)$ if and only if $M = \mathbb{I}_n \otimes A - B^T \otimes \mathbb{I}_m$ is invertible. By diagonalization of $A$ and $B$ on the left space and right space respectively, we conclude this is satisfied iff $\text{spec}(A) \cap \text{spec}(B) = \emptyset$.
:::

:::{#lem-direct-rotation .callout-important icon="false"}
## Direct rotation and its generator
Given two projectors $P, P_0$, if $\|{P} - {P}_0\| <1$, then:

- (i).$\text{dim~}\mathcal{P}_0 =\text{dim~}\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{P}_0 \not\subset \mathcal{P}^\perp,\mathcal{P}\not\subset\mathcal{P}_0^\perp$. 
- (ii).There exists $U = \sqrt{(2P_0-\mathbb{I})(2P-\mathbb{I})}$ such that $UPU^\dagger = P_0$. 
- (iii).The unitary matrix can be uniquely written as $e^{S}$ .
Here $S$ is the generator of the direct rotation, which satisfies the conditions $S^\dagger = -S$,$PSP = P_0SP_0 = (I − P )S(I − P ) = (I − P_0)S(I − P_0) = 0$, and $\|S\| < \pi/2$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch (Click to expand)
*(Following @bravyi2011schrieffer, Lemma 2.2, Corollary 2.2, and Lemma 2.3)*

**(i) Equal dimensions.** Any pair of projectors $P, P_0$ can be simultaneously block-diagonalized into $2 \times 2$ and $1 \times 1$ blocks, with each $2 \times 2$ block containing rank-one projectors [see @bhatia1997matrix, Chapter 7.1]. In each $1 \times 1$ block, $\|P - P_0\| < 1$ forces $P = P_0 \in \{0, 1\}$. In each $2 \times 2$ block, both $P$ and $P_0$ are rank-one projectors (so non-orthogonality is guaranteed), contributing equally to $\dim \mathcal{P}$ and $\dim \mathcal{P}_0$.

**(ii) Existence of $U$.** Define reflection operators $R_P = 2P - \mathbb{I}$, $R_{P_0} = 2P_0 - \mathbb{I}$, and $U = \sqrt{R_{P_0} R_P}$ with the principal branch of the square root. The condition $\|P - P_0\| < 1$ ensures no eigenvalue of $R_{P_0} R_P$ lies on the negative real axis, so $U$ is uniquely defined. Within each $2 \times 2$ block, the rotation reduces to $U = e^{i\theta \sigma_y}$ (with $0 \le \theta < \pi/2$) which maps the rank-one projector $P$ to $P_0$, giving $U P U^\dagger = P_0$.

**(iii) Uniqueness of $S$.** Write $U = e^S$ with $S$ block-off-diagonal w.r.t. $P_0$. In the $P_0 / P_0^\perp$ block decomposition, $U_{1,1} = \cos(\sqrt{S_{1,2} S_{1,2}^\dagger})$ and $U_{2,2} = \cos(\sqrt{S_{1,2}^\dagger S_{1,2}})$. Since $\|S\| < \pi/2$, both are positive-definite. If another $\tilde{U} = e^{\tilde{S}}$ also satisfies the conditions, then $L = \tilde{U}U^\dagger$ commutes with $P_0$ (hence block-diagonal). The relation $\tilde{U}_{1,1} = L_1 U_{1,1}$ with both sides positive-definite forces $L_1 = \mathbb{I}$ (a unitary times a positive-definite operator is positive only if the unitary is the identity). Similarly $L_2 = \mathbb{I}$, so $\tilde{U} = U$. Injectivity of $\exp$ on $\|S\| < \pi/2$ then gives $\tilde{S} = S$. $\square$
:::

Based on the discussion above, the effective Hamiltonian is defined as 
$$
\boxed{H_{\mathrm{eff}} := P_0U(H_0 + \varepsilon V)U^\dagger P_0}
$$
Intuitatively, the value of effective Hamiltonian ensures that given $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal{P}$, solving its evolution in time according to $H$ 
is precisely equivalnent to tracing $\ket{\phi} =U\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal{P}_0$ evolution according to  $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
In the same reference [@bravyi2011schrieffer], it is also shown how to approximate $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$ in terms of Taylor series of $\varepsilon$, which is concluded in @lem-perturbation_expand.

:::{#lem-perturbation_expand .callout-important icon="false"}
## Perturbative expansion of $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (@bravyi2011schrieffer, Section 3.2)
Given the Hamiltonian $H = H_0 + \varepsilon V$ and the low-energy subspace of interest with projector $P_0$. Let the superoperator $\mathcal{L}$ be defined as
$$
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{L}(\cdot) = \sum_{i,j} \frac{\bra{i} \mathcal{O}(\cdot) \ket{j}}{E_i - E_j} \ket{i}\!\bra{j},
\end{align}
$$
where $\ket{i}$ are the eigenvectors of the free Hamiltonian such that $H_0\ket{i} = E_i \ket{i}$. The map $\mathcal{O}(\cdot) = P_0 (\cdot)(\mathbb{I}-P_0) + (\mathbb{I}-P_0)(\cdot)P_0$ retains only the off-diagonal terms, and $\hat{A}(\cdot) = [A, \cdot]$ is the commutator linear transformation. Then the effective Hamiltonian is given by
$$
\begin{align}
    H_{\mathrm{eff}} = H_0 P_0 + \epsilon P_0 V P_0 + \frac{\epsilon^2}{2} P_0 \hat{S}_1(V_{od}) P_0 + \frac{\epsilon^3}{2} P_0 \hat{V}_{od} \mathcal{L} \hat{V}_d(S_1) P_0 + O(\epsilon^4),
\end{align}
$$
where $S_1 := \mathcal{L}(V_{\mathrm{od}}), V_{\mathrm{od}} = \mathcal{O}(V)$ and $V_{\mathrm{d}} = V - V_{\mathrm{od}}$. 
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch (Click to expand)
 Write $U = e^S$ with $S$ block-off-diagonal w.r.t. $P_0$. The transformed Hamiltonian $e^{\hat{S}}(H_0 + \epsilon V)$ (where $\hat{S}(\cdot) = [S, \cdot]$) decomposes into block-diagonal (BD) and block-off-diagonal (BOD) parts:
$$
e^{\hat{S}}(H_0 + \epsilon V) = \underbrace{\cosh(\hat{S})(H_0 + \epsilon V_d) + \sinh(\hat{S})(\epsilon V_{od})}_{\text{BD}} + \underbrace{\sinh(\hat{S})(H_0 + \epsilon V_d) + \cosh(\hat{S})(\epsilon V_{od})}_{\text{BOD}}.
$$
Setting the BOD part to zero and dividing by $\cosh(\hat{S})$ yields:
$$
\tanh(\hat{S})(H_0 + \epsilon V_d) + \epsilon V_{od} = 0.
$$

The superoperator $\mathcal{L}$ satisfies $\mathcal{L}([H_0, X]) = \mathcal{O}(X)$, which means
$$
\mathcal L\hat H_0(X)=X \quad \text{for BOD }X,
$$
Expanding $S = \sum_{n \geq 1} S_n \epsilon^n$ and solving order by order:
$$
S_1 = \mathcal{L}(V_{od}), \quad S_2 = -\mathcal{L}\hat{V}_d(S_1), \quad S_n = -\mathcal{L}\hat{V}_d(S_{n-1}) + \text{(higher-order corrections from } x\coth(x) \text{)}.
$$

Using the identity $\sinh(x) - \frac{\cosh(x) - 1}{\tanh(x)} = \tanh(x/2)$, the BD transformed Hamiltonian simplifies to:
$$
e^{\hat{S}}(H_0 + \epsilon V) = H_0 + \epsilon V_d + \tanh(\hat{S}/2)(\epsilon V_{od}).
$$
Since $H_0$ and $V_d$ are BD, $P_0 V_d P_0 = P_0 V P_0$. Expanding $\tanh(x/2) = \sum_{n \geq 1} b_{2n-1} x^{2n-1}$ with $b_1 = 1/2$, $b_3 = -1/24$, etc., the $n$-th order correction is $H_{\mathrm{eff},n} = \sum_{j \geq 1} b_{2j-1} P_0 \hat{S}^{2j-1}(V_{od})_{n-1} P_0$. The leading terms are:

- $H_{\mathrm{eff},2} = \frac{1}{2} P_0 \hat{S}_1(V_{od}) P_0 = \frac{1}{2} P_0 [S_1, V_{od}] P_0$
- $H_{\mathrm{eff},3} = \frac{1}{2} P_0 \hat{V}_{od} \mathcal{L}\hat{V}_d(S_1) P_0$

Combining all orders gives the stated formula. $\square$
:::
